scenes.heading: narratr

steps.label: Document
steps.cue: You point it at a document

scenes.narration: Narrator turns a document into a narrated video, and it runs entirely on your own machine. You point it at a document, it writes the script, and your laptop does the rest.

scenes.heading: The usual failure
scenes.narration: Every project like this fails the same way. You build the slides first, then try to make the narration fit them. The timing drifts, and every edit breaks the alignment all over again.

scenes.heading: Where the clock comes from
scenes.narration: Narration is rendered first, and it is measured. Those measurements go two ways at once: into the word timings that become captions, and into the length each scene is drawn to fit. Assembly joins the two back together.

scenes.heading: What it costs

cards.title: Twice the runtime
cards.detail: A 2 min clip costs about 4 min
cards.cue: What you pay instead is time

cards.title: Nothing leaves
cards.cue: Every stage runs on your own machine

scenes.narration: A video costs nothing to make. There is no subscription and no metered API. What you pay instead is time, at roughly twice the length of the finished video, and none of it needs you watching. Every stage runs on your own machine, so nothing is uploaded.

scenes.heading: Starting a run
scenes.narration: One command starts it. Detaching returns a run identifier in about a second and keeps rendering after the session that started it has gone away.

scenes.heading: Where it stands
scenes.narration: Runs checkpoint after every scene, so a closed laptop lid costs ninety seconds rather than the afternoon. And because everything is cached by content, editing one slide costs seconds rather than a rebuild.
